content: Magnesium is a vital mineral that plays a critical role in regulating body temperature, synthesizing nucleic acids and proteins, and maintaining the electrical potentials of nerve and muscle cells. Many women, particularly those from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds, have insufficient magnesium intake. Supplementing magnesium during pregnancy has been hypothesized to potentially reduce the risk of fetal growth restriction and pre-eclampsia, as well as to increase birthweight. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of magnesium supplementation during pregnancy on maternal, neonatal, infant, and pediatric outcomes. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that assessed dietary magnesium supplementation in pregnant women. The primary outcomes of interest were perinatal mortality (including stillbirth and neonatal death before hospital discharge), small-for-gestational-age infants, maternal mortality, and pre-eclampsia. The review included 10 trials involving a total of 9,090 women and their babies. One of these trials used a cluster design, with randomization occurring at the study center level. In all 10 trials, participants were randomly assigned to receive either an oral magnesium supplement or a control intervention. Eight trials used a placebo as the control, while two trials provided no treatment to the control group. The magnesium supplements varied in composition, dosage, and timing of administration. For example, magnesium oxide was administered at 1,000 mg daily starting from ≤4 months post-conception in one trial, while magnesium citrate was given at 365 mg daily from ≤18 weeks until hospitalization after 38 weeks in another. Other forms of magnesium used included magnesium gluconate, magnesium aspartate, and magnesium stearate, with doses ranging from 128 mg to 4 g daily and initiation times spanning from <12 weeks to 28 weeks of gestation. When all trials were analyzed together, oral magnesium supplementation did not result in significant differences in perinatal mortality (risk ratio [RR] 1.10; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.72 to 1.67; five trials, 5,903 infants), small-for-gestational-age infants (RR 0.76; 95% CI 0.54 to 1.07; three trials, 1,291 infants), or pre-eclampsia (RR 0.87; 95% CI 0.58 to 1.32; three trials, 1,042 women). None of the included trials reported maternal mortality as an outcome. Regarding secondary outcomes, no increased risk of stillbirth was observed. However, there was a potential increased risk of neonatal death before hospital discharge among infants born to mothers who received magnesium supplementation (RR 2.21; 95% CI 1.02 to 4.75; four trials, 5,373 infants). This finding was heavily influenced by one trial, which contributed over 70% of the participants to this analysis. The authors of that trial suggested that the observed increased risk of neonatal death might be explained by a high number of severe congenital anomalies in the supplemented group (which were unlikely to be related to magnesium) and the deaths of two sets of twins with extremely low birthweights (<750 g). When deaths due to severe congenital abnormalities were excluded from the meta-analysis, the increased risk of neonatal death was no longer observed. Magnesium supplementation was associated with several positive secondary outcomes. Babies born to mothers who received magnesium were significantly less likely to have an Apgar score below seven at five minutes (RR 0.34; 95% CI 0.15 to 0.80; four trials, 1,083 infants). There was also a reduced likelihood of meconium-stained amniotic fluid (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.99; one trial, 4,082 infants), late fetal heart rate decelerations (RR 0.68; 95% CI 0.53 to 0.88; one trial, 4,082 infants), and mild hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (RR 0.38; 95% CI 0.15 to 0.98; one trial, 4,082 infants). Additionally, women who received magnesium supplementation were significantly less likely to require hospitalization during pregnancy (RR 0.65; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.86; three trials, 1,158 women). Of the 10 trials included in the review, only two were judged to be of high methodological quality. When the analysis was restricted to these two high-quality trials, none of the primary outcomes (perinatal mortality, small-for-gestational-age infants, or pre-eclampsia) showed significant differences between the magnesium-supplemented and control groups. In conclusion, there is insufficient high-quality evidence to support the routine use of dietary magnesium supplementation during pregnancy as a beneficial intervention.
